---
title: "Institutions"
subtitle: "Who shapes Adamsville, and who is left out of the room"
---

Adamsville's institutions are many but thinly connected. Formal power sits with the city and with the agencies that fund development. Informal influence runs through churches, elders and personal relationships. The residents with the least access to either are renters and young families.

## The institutional map

The diagram sorts Adamsville's institutions by the kind of power they hold. Formal power (rules and money) is at the top, the organizations that broker services and voice are in the middle, and residents are at the bottom. **Click any box** to see its role, power, incentive and how residents experience it; its connections stay highlighted. Solid lines are formal, regular relationships. Dashed lines are weak or occasional ones.

*Sources: interviews with Residents A and B (October 2026); City of Atlanta & TSW (2020); Invest Atlanta (2025a, 2025b); Atlanta News First (2022); Daniel (2025).*

## Incentives that pull in different directions

**Development money depends on rising values.** The Hollowell/MLK Tax Allocation District, created in 2006, funds projects by capturing growth in property tax revenue along the MLK corridor, and lists "Adamsville Village" as a development site (Invest Atlanta, 2025b). In 2025 the mayor announced a $5.1 billion Neighborhood Reinvestment Initiative for south and west Atlanta that includes this district (WSB-TV, 2025). This is the tool that paid for the food center, with $250,000 from the TAD and a $250,000 Invest Atlanta grant (Invest Atlanta, 2025a). But the mechanism works best when property values climb, and rising values are what long-time owners on fixed incomes and cost-burdened renters fear.

**Schools follow enrollment.** In 2022 Atlanta Public Schools reopened the old Margaret Fain Elementary building, which the Civic Club called "the most important building in the community" in 1955, as a ninth-grade campus for Douglass High School. In late 2025 APS adopted a facilities plan that closes that building, saving about $500,000 a year (Atlanta News First, 2022; Daniel, 2025). Resident A noticed the effect right away: "the youth aren't as busy over here as much."

**The NPU runs on volunteers.** NPU-H's chair, Khalifa S. Lee, is widely credited with its energy. Resident B called NPU-H "one of the most active" in the city, and Lee pointed to the master plan when the food center opened: "We have in our master plan that we wanted food banks all across our area" (Andrews, 2025). But the plan shows the limits of volunteer capacity. Its 2019 survey drew 38 responses from an area of about 16,000 people, and steering committee attendance fell from 13 members to 5 between the first two meetings (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, pp. 53–58).

::: {.voice}
"The struggle is how do you engage community without like a incentive. Like, what's in it for me if I come to these meetings?"
<span class="who">Resident A, NPU-H volunteer, interview, October 16, 2026</span>
:::

## Who is represented, and what it costs those who are not

**Elders are heard, and residents want it that way.** Resident B explained that in meetings "people respect their elders here… their voices are prioritized. And I actually think they should be."

**Renters and working parents are not.** Renters make up 54 percent of NPU-H households, but both residents described meetings attended by the same homeowners and board members. Resident B, a working parent, joins "usually multitasking," and said it is "like pulling teeth to get people to go." The master plan names the gap: one housing goal is to "engage renters in the community and encourage them to stay" (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, p. 69). The consequence is concrete. The issues raised most at meetings are homeowner issues such as streetlights, signage and flooding. Child poverty of 44 percent and a renter cost burden of 57 percent rarely surface in the meeting room.

**Access depends on personal connections.** Resident B described a sewage smell on her street that the city addressed only after a week of calls, leaving large holes in the road. The holes were filled within a week of her mentioning them to a city official she knows personally. Resident A described a related gap: "the only people that really enforce anything in Adamsville are like code enforcers or police. There's no like middle person."

**Absentee owners hold quiet power.** Resident A sees homes being renovated and listed "for rent, like Airbnb," bringing "strangers into the community" while raising property values. Georgia Tech's Brian An found that large investors bought up to 76 percent of homes for sale in some metro Atlanta neighborhoods between 2007 and 2016, mostly in majority-minority areas, and accounted for most of the decline in Black homeownership (An, 2023). In Fulton County, large corporate landlords were 68 percent more likely than small landlords to file evictions (Raymond et al., 2018). Investors and short-term rental operators have no seat at NPU-H, yet their decisions shape who can stay.
